statement: When the digit 1 is written in front of a two-digit number, the new three-digit number is exactly 5 times the original number. What is the sum of the digits of the original number?

choices.misconception: I added the digits of the new three-digit number, 125, instead of the original one.
I added the digits of both numbers, 25 and 125, together.
I found the original number and gave it instead of the sum of its digits.
I gave the new three-digit number instead of anything about the original.

hints: What does writing a 1 in front of a two-digit number add to it?
Writing 1 in the hundreds place adds exactly 100, so the new number is the old number plus 100. Use the fact that it is also 5 times the old number.
The old number plus 100 equals 5 times the old number, so 100 must be 4 times the old number.

solutions.reliable: Writing the digit 1 in front of a two-digit number puts 1 in the hundreds place, which adds 100. So the new number is (original + 100). It is also 5 times the original, so original + 100 = 5 × original, which means 100 = 4 × original, and the original is 25. Check: writing 1 in front gives 125, and 5 × 25 = 125. The digit sum of 25 is 2 + 5 = 7. The transferable idea: a digit placed in a position adds its place value, so turn a digit trick into "number plus place value".
solutions.elegant: Think of the new number as five copies of the old one. One copy is already inside it, so the other four copies must make up the extra 100, and each copy is 25.

whyOnTest: Place value puzzles test whether you see that a digit in the hundreds place simply adds a hundred-sized chunk.
